findings.name: Microsoft Windows Remote Listeners Enumeration (WMI)
findings.synopsis: It is possible to obtain the names of processes listening on the remote UDP and TCP ports.
findings.description: This script uses WMI to list the processes running on the remote host and listening on TCP / UDP ports.

findings.name: Netstat Portscanner (WMI)
findings.synopsis: Remote open ports can be enumerated via WMI.
findings.description: Using the WMI interface, Nessus was able to run 'netstat' on the remote host to enumerate the open ports.

findings.name: DCE Services Enumeration
findings.synopsis: A DCE/RPC service is running on the remote host.
findings.description: By sending a Lookup request to the portmapper (TCP 135 or epmapper PIPE) it was possible to enumerate the Distributed Computing Environment (DCE) services running on the remote port. Using this information it is possible to connect and bind to each service by sending an RPC request to the remote port/pipe.

findings.name: HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Information
findings.synopsis: Some information about the remote HTTP configuration can be extracted.
findings.description:
This test gives some information about the remote HTTP protocol - the version used, whether HTTP Keep-Alive is enabled, etc... 

This test is informational only and does not denote any security problem.

findings.name: HTTP Server Type and Version
findings.synopsis: A web server is running on the remote host.
findings.description: This plugin attempts to determine the type and the version of the   remote web server.

findings.name: Service Detection
findings.synopsis: The remote service could be identified.
findings.description: Nessus was able to identify the remote service by its banner or by looking at the error message it sends when it receives an HTTP request.

findings.name: SSL Perfect Forward Secrecy Cipher Suites Supported
findings.synopsis: The remote service supports the use of SSL Perfect Forward Secrecy ciphers, which maintain confidentiality even if the key is stolen.
findings.description: The remote host supports the use of SSL ciphers that offer Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) encryption.  These cipher suites ensure that recorded SSL traffic cannot be broken at a future date if the server's private key is compromised.

findings.name: TLS Version 1.2 Protocol Detection
findings.synopsis: The remote service encrypts traffic using a version of TLS.
findings.description: The remote service accepts connections encrypted using TLS 1.2.

findings.name: SSL Self-Signed Certificate
findings.synopsis: The SSL certificate chain for this service ends in an unrecognized self-signed certificate.
findings.description:
The X.509 certificate chain for this service is not signed by a recognized certificate authority.  If the remote host is a public host in production, this nullifies the use of SSL as anyone could establish a man-in-the-middle attack against the remote host. 

Note that this plugin does not check for certificate chains that end in a certificate that is not self-signed, but is signed by an unrecognized certificate authority.
findings.solution: Purchase or generate a proper SSL certificate for this service.

findings.name: SSL Certificate Cannot Be Trusted
findings.synopsis: The SSL certificate for this service cannot be trusted.
findings.description:
The server's X.509 certificate cannot be trusted. This situation can occur in three different ways, in which the chain of trust can be broken, as stated below :

  - First, the top of the certificate chain sent by the     server might not be descended from a known public     certificate authority. This can occur either when the     top of the chain is an unrecognized, self-signed     certificate, or when intermediate certificates are     missing that would connect the top of the certificate     chain to a known public certificate authority.

  - Second, the certificate chain may contain a certificate     that is not valid at the time of the scan. This can     occur either when the scan occurs before one of the     certificate's 'notBefore' dates, or after one of the     certificate's 'notAfter' dates.

  - Third, the certificate chain may contain a signature     that either didn't match the certificate's information     or could not be verified. Bad signatures can be fixed by     getting the certificate with the bad signature to be     re-signed by its issuer. Signatures that could not be     verified are the result of the certificate's issuer     using a signing algorithm that Nessus either does not     support or does not recognize.

If the remote host is a public host in production, any break in the chain makes it more difficult for users to verify the authenticity and identity of the web server. This could make it easier to carry out man-in-the-middle attacks against the remote host.
findings.solution: Purchase or generate a proper SSL certificate for this service.

findings.name: SSL Certificate with Wrong Hostname
findings.synopsis: The SSL certificate for this service is for a different host.
findings.description: The 'commonName' (CN) attribute of the SSL certificate presented for this service is for a different machine.
findings.solution: Purchase or generate a proper SSL certificate for this service.

findings.name: SSL Certificate 'commonName' Mismatch
findings.synopsis: The 'commonName' (CN) attribute in the SSL certificate does not match the hostname.
findings.description: The service running on the remote host presents an SSL certificate for which the 'commonName' (CN) attribute does not match the hostname on which the service listens.
findings.solution: If the machine has several names, make sure that users connect to the service through the DNS hostname that matches the common name in the certificate.

findings.name: SSL Certificate Information
findings.synopsis: This plugin displays the SSL certificate.
findings.description: This plugin connects to every SSL-related port and attempts to extract and dump the X.509 certificate.

findings.name: SSL Cipher Suites Supported
findings.synopsis: The remote service encrypts communications using SSL.
findings.description: This plugin detects which SSL ciphers are supported by the remote service for encrypting communications.

findings.name: SSL / TLS Versions Supported
findings.synopsis: The remote service encrypts communications.
findings.description: This plugin detects which SSL and TLS versions are supported by the remote service for encrypting communications.

findings.name: WS-Management Server Detection
findings.synopsis: The remote web server is used for remote management.
findings.description: The remote web server supports the Web Services for Management (WS-Management) specification, a general web services protocol based on SOAP for managing systems, applications, and other such entities.
findings.solution: Limit incoming traffic to this port if desired.

findings.name: TLS Version 1.3 Protocol Detection
findings.synopsis: The remote service encrypts traffic using a version of TLS.
findings.description: The remote service accepts connections encrypted using TLS 1.3.

findings.name: SSL Certificate with no Common Name
findings.synopsis: Checks for an SSL certificate with no Common Name
findings.description: The remote system is providing an SSL/TLS certificate without a subject common name field. While this is not required in all cases, it is recommended to ensure broad compatibility.

findings.name: Terminal Services Doesn't Use Network Level Authentication (NLA) Only
findings.synopsis: The remote Terminal Services doesn't use Network Level Authentication only.
findings.description: The remote Terminal Services is not configured to use Network Level Authentication (NLA) only. NLA uses the Credential Security Support Provider (CredSSP) protocol to perform strong server authentication either through TLS/SSL or Kerberos mechanisms, which protect against man-in-the-middle attacks. In addition to improving authentication, NLA also helps protect the remote computer from malicious users and software by completing user authentication before a full RDP connection is established.
findings.solution: Enable Network Level Authentication (NLA) on the remote RDP server. This is generally done on the 'Remote' tab of the 'System' settings on Windows.

findings.name: SSL Cipher Block Chaining Cipher Suites Supported
findings.synopsis: The remote service supports the use of SSL Cipher Block Chaining ciphers, which combine previous blocks with subsequent ones.
findings.description: The remote host supports the use of SSL ciphers that operate in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode.  These cipher suites offer additional security over Electronic Codebook (ECB) mode, but have the potential to leak information if used improperly.

findings.name: SSL Medium Strength Cipher Suites Supported (SWEET32)
findings.synopsis: The remote service supports the use of medium strength SSL ciphers.
findings.description:
The remote host supports the use of SSL ciphers that offer medium strength encryption. Nessus regards medium strength as any encryption that uses key lengths at least 64 bits and less than 112 bits, or else that uses the 3DES encryption suite.

Note that it is considerably easier to circumvent medium strength encryption if the attacker is on the same physical network.
findings.solution: Reconfigure the affected application if possible to avoid use of medium strength ciphers.

findings.name: SSL/TLS Recommended Cipher Suites
findings.synopsis: The remote host advertises discouraged SSL/TLS ciphers.
findings.description:
The remote host has open SSL/TLS ports which advertise discouraged cipher suites. It is recommended to only enable support for the following cipher suites:

TLSv1.3:
  - 0x13,0x01 TLS13_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
  - 0x13,0x02 TLS13_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
  - 0x13,0x03 TLS13_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256

TLSv1.2:
  - 0xC0,0x2B ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256
  - 0xC0,0x2F ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256
  - 0xC0,0x2C ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384
  - 0xC0,0x30 ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384
  - 0xCC,0xA9 ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305
  - 0xCC,0xA8 ECDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305

This is the recommended configuration for the vast majority of services, as it is highly secure and compatible with nearly every client released in the last five (or more) years.
findings.solution: Only enable support for recommened cipher suites.

findings.name: SSL RC4 Cipher Suites Supported (Bar Mitzvah)
findings.synopsis: The remote service supports the use of the RC4 cipher.
findings.description:
The remote host supports the use of RC4 in one or more cipher suites.
The RC4 cipher is flawed in its generation of a pseudo-random stream of bytes so that a wide variety of small biases are introduced into the stream, decreasing its randomness.

If plaintext is repeatedly encrypted (e.g., HTTP cookies), and an attacker is able to obtain many (i.e., tens of millions) ciphertexts, the attacker may be able to derive the plaintext.
findings.solution: Reconfigure the affected application, if possible, to avoid use of RC4 ciphers. Consider using TLS 1.2 with AES-GCM suites subject to browser and web server support.

findings.name: TLS Version 1.1 Deprecated Protocol
findings.synopsis: The remote service encrypts traffic using an older version of TLS.
findings.description:
The remote service accepts connections encrypted using TLS 1.1. TLS 1.1 lacks support for current and recommended cipher suites. Ciphers that support encryption before MAC computation, and authenticated encryption modes such as GCM cannot be used with TLS 1.1

As of March 31, 2020, Endpoints that are not enabled for TLS 1.2 and higher will no longer function properly with major web browsers and major vendors.
findings.solution: Enable support for TLS 1.2 and/or 1.3, and disable support for TLS 1.1.

findings.name: TLS Version 1.0 Protocol Detection
findings.synopsis: The remote service encrypts traffic using an older version of TLS.
findings.description:
The remote service accepts connections encrypted using TLS 1.0. TLS 1.0 has a number of cryptographic design flaws. Modern implementations of TLS 1.0 mitigate these problems, but newer versions of TLS like 1.2 and 1.3 are designed against these flaws and should be used whenever possible.

As of March 31, 2020, Endpoints that aren’t enabled for TLS 1.2 and higher will no longer function properly with major web browsers and major vendors.

PCI DSS v3.2 requires that TLS 1.0 be disabled entirely by June 30, 2018, except for POS POI terminals (and the SSL/TLS termination points to which they connect) that can be verified as not being susceptible to any known exploits.
findings.solution: Enable support for TLS 1.2 and 1.3, and disable support for TLS 1.0.

findings.name: TLS Version 1.1 Protocol Detection
findings.synopsis: The remote service encrypts traffic using an older version of TLS.
findings.description:
The remote service accepts connections encrypted using TLS 1.1.
TLS 1.1 lacks support for current and recommended cipher suites.
Ciphers that support encryption before MAC computation, and authenticated encryption modes such as GCM cannot be used with TLS 1.1

As of March 31, 2020, Endpoints that are not enabled for TLS 1.2 and higher will no longer function properly with major web browsers and major vendors.
findings.solution: Enable support for TLS 1.2 and/or 1.3, and disable support for TLS 1.1.

findings.name: Terminal Services Use SSL/TLS
findings.synopsis: The remote Terminal Services use SSL/TLS.
findings.description: The remote Terminal Services is configured to use SSL/TLS.

findings.name: Remote Desktop Protocol Service Detection
findings.synopsis: The remote host has an remote desktop protocol service enabled.
findings.description:
The Remote Desktop Protocol allows a user to remotely obtain a graphical login (and therefore act as a local user on the remote host).

If an attacker gains a valid login and password, this service could be used to gain further access on the remote host.  An attacker may also use this service to mount a dictionary attack against the remote host to try to log in remotely.

Note that RDP (the Remote Desktop Protocol) is vulnerable to Man-in-the-middle attacks, making it easy for attackers to steal the credentials of legitimate users by impersonating the Windows server.
findings.solution: Disable the service if you do not use it, and do not allow this service to run across the Internet.

findings.name: Service Detection (GET request)
findings.synopsis: The remote service could be identified.
findings.description: It was possible to identify the remote service by its banner or by looking at the error message it sends when it receives an HTTP request.

findings.name: Target Credential Issues by Authentication Protocol - Intermittent Authentication Failure
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to log in to the remote host using the provided credentials, but there were intermittent authentication failures.
findings.description:
Nessus was able to successfully authenticate to the remote host on an authentication protocol at least once using credentials provided in the scan policy.

However, one or more plugins failed to authenticate to the remote host on the same port and protocol using the same credential set that was previously successful. This may indicate an intermittent authentication problem with the remote host, which could be caused by session rate limits, session concurrency limits, or other issues preventing consistent authentication success.

These intermittent authentication failures may have affected the results of some plugins. See plugin output for failure details.

findings.name: Target Credential Status by Authentication Protocol - Valid Credentials Provided
findings.synopsis: Valid credentials were provided for an available authentication protocol.
findings.description:
Nessus was able to determine that valid credentials were provided for an authentication protocol available on the remote target because it was able to successfully authenticate directly to the remote target using that authentication protocol at least once. Authentication was successful because the authentication protocol service was available remotely, the service was able to be identified, the authentication protocol was able to be negotiated successfully, and a set of credentials provided in the scan policy for that authentication protocol was accepted by the remote service. See plugin output for details, including protocol, port, and account.

Please note the following :

- This plugin reports per protocol, so it is possible for   valid credentials to be provided for one protocol and not   another. For example, authentication may succeed via SSH   but fail via SMB, while no credentials were provided for   an available SNMP service.

- Providing valid credentials for all available   authentication protocols may improve scan coverage, but   the value of successful authentication for a given   protocol may vary from target to target depending upon   what data (if any) is gathered from the target via that   protocol. For example, successful authentication via SSH   is more valuable for Linux targets than for Windows   targets, and likewise successful authentication via SMB   is more valuable for Windows targets than for Linux   targets.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Summary of Missing Patches
findings.synopsis: The remote host is missing several Microsoft security patches.
findings.description:
This plugin summarizes updates for Microsoft Security Bulletins or Knowledge Base (KB) security updates that have not been installed on the remote Windows host based on the results of either a credentialed check using the supplied credentials or a check done using a supported third-party patch management tool.

Note the results of missing patches also include superseded patches.

Review the summary and apply any missing updates in order to be up to date.
findings.solution: Run Windows Update on the remote host or use a patch management solution.

findings.name: OS Security Patch Assessment Available
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to log in to the remote host using the provided credentials and enumerate OS security patch levels.
findings.description: Nessus was able to determine OS security patch levels by logging into the remote host and running commands to determine the version of the operating system and its components.  The remote host was identified as an operating system or device that Nessus supports for patch and update assessment.  The necessary information was obtained to perform these checks.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB2 and SMB3 Dialects Supported (remote check)
findings.synopsis: It was possible to obtain information about the dialects of SMB2 and SMB3 available on the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to obtain the set of SMB2 and SMB3 dialects running on the remote host by sending an authentication request to port 139 or 445.

findings.name: Server Message Block (SMB) Protocol Version Detection
findings.synopsis: Verify the version of SMB on the remote host.
findings.description: The Server Message Block (SMB) Protocol provides   shared access to files and printers across nodes   on a network.
findings.solution: Disable SMB version 1 and block all versions of SMB at   the network boundary by blocking TCP port 445 with   related protocols on UDP ports 137-138 and TCP port 139,   for all boundary devices.

findings.name: Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) Service Detection
findings.synopsis: Verify status of the LLMNR service on the remote host.
findings.description: The Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) service   allows both IPv4 and IPv6 hosts to perform name resolution   for hosts on the same local link
findings.solution: Make sure that use of this software conforms to your organization's   acceptable use and security policies.

findings.name: Windows Credential Guard Status
findings.synopsis: Retrieves the status of Windows Credential Guard.
findings.description:
Retrieves the status of Windows Credential Guard.
  Credential Guard prevents attacks such as such as Pass-the-Hash or   Pass-The-Ticket by protecting NTLM password hashes, Kerberos Ticket   Granting Tickets, and credentials stored by applications as domain   credentials.

findings.name: Windows LSA Protection Status
findings.synopsis: Windows LSA Protection is disabled on the remote Windows host.
findings.description: The LSA Protection validates users for local and remote sign-ins   and enforces local security policies to prevent reading memory and code injection by non-protected processes.   This provides added security for the credentials that the LSA stores and manages. This protects against Pass-the-Hash   or Mimikatz-style attacks.
findings.solution: Enable LSA Protection per your corporate security guidelines.

findings.name: Windows Services Registry ACL
findings.synopsis: Checks Windows Registry for Service ACLs
findings.description: Checks Windows Registry for Service ACLs.

findings.name: Windows Always Installed Elevated Status
findings.synopsis: Windows AlwaysInstallElevated policy status was found on the remote Windows host
findings.description:
Windows AlwaysInstallElevated policy status was found on the remote Windows host.
  You can use the AlwaysInstallElevated policy to install a Windows Installer package with elevated (system) privileges   This option is equivalent to granting full administrative rights, which can pose a massive security risk. Microsoft strongly discourages the use of this setting.
findings.solution: If enabled, disable AlwaysInstallElevated policy per your corporate security guidelines.

findings.name: MS17-013: Security Update for Microsoft Graphics Component (4013075)
findings.synopsis: The remote Windows host is affected by multiple vulnerabilities.
findings.description:
The remote Windows host is missing a security update. It is, therefore, affected by multiple vulnerabilities :

  - Multiple elevation of privilege vulnerabilities exist in     the Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI) component     due to improper handling of objects in memory. A local     attacker can exploit these vulnerabilities, via a     specially crafted application, to execute arbitrary code     in kernel mode. (CVE-2017-0001, CVE-2017-0005,     CVE-2017-0025, CVE-2017-0047)

  - Multiple remote code execution vulnerabilities exist in     the Windows Graphics component due to improper handling     of objects in memory. An unauthenticated, remote     attacker can exploit these vulnerabilities, by     convincing a user to visit a specially crafted web page     or open a specially crafted document, to execute     arbitrary code. (CVE-2017-0014, CVE-2017-0108)

  - An information disclosure vulnerability exists in the     Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI) component due to     improper handling of objects in memory. An     unauthenticated, remote attacker can exploit this, by     convincing a user to visit a specially crafted web page     or open a specially crafted document, to disclose the     contents of memory. (CVE-2017-0038)

  - Multiple information disclosure vulnerabilities exist in     the Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI) component     due to improper handling of memory addresses. A local     attacker can exploit these vulnerabilities, via a     specially crafted application, to disclose sensitive     information. (CVE-2017-0060, CVE-2017-0062,     CVE-2017-0073)

  - Multiple information disclosure vulnerabilities exist in     the Color Management Module (ICM32.dll) due to improper     handling of objects in memory. An unauthenticated,     remote attacker can exploit this, by convincing a user     to visit a specially crafted web page, to disclose     sensitive information and bypass usermode Address Space     Layout Randomization (ASLR). (CVE-2017-0061,     CVE-2017-0063)
findings.solution:
Microsoft has released a set of patches for Windows XP, 2003, Vista, 2008, 7, 2008 R2, 2012, 8.1, RT 8.1, 2012 R2, 10, and 2016.
Additionally, Microsoft has released a set of patches for Office 2007, Office 2010, Word Viewer, Skype for Business 2016, Lync 2010, Lync 2010 Attendee, Lync 2013, Lync Basic 2013, Live Meeting 2007 Console, and Silverlight 5.

findings.name: Windows 10 / Windows Server 2016 September 2017 Information Disclosure Vulnerability (CVE-2017-8529)
findings.synopsis: The remote Windows host is affected by an information disclosure vulnerability.
findings.description:
The remote Windows host is missing a security update or a registry setting required to enable protections for CVE-2017-8529. It is, therefore, affected by an information disclosure vulnerability:

- An information disclosure vulnerability exists when affected Microsoft scripting engines do not properly handle objects in memory. The vulnerability could allow an attacker to detect specific files on the user's computer. In a web-based attack scenario, an attacker could host a website that is used to attempt to exploit the vulnerability.
findings.solution: Refer to the Microsoft CVE article for additional information.

findings.name: Microsoft Patch Bulletin Feasibility Check
findings.synopsis: Nessus is able to check for Microsoft patch bulletins.
findings.description:
Using credentials supplied in the scan policy, Nessus is able to collect information about the software and patches installed on the remote Windows host and will use that information to check for missing Microsoft security updates.

Note that this plugin is purely informational.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB Versions Supported (remote check)
findings.synopsis: It was possible to obtain information about the version of SMB running on the remote host.
findings.description:
Nessus was able to obtain the version of SMB running on the remote host by sending an authentication request to port 139 or 445.

Note that this plugin is a remote check and does not work on agents.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Print Spooler Service Enabled
findings.synopsis: The Microsoft Windows Print Spooler service on the remote host is enabled.
findings.description: The Microsoft Windows Print Spooler service (spoolsv.exe) on the remote host is enabled.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB Service Config Enumeration
findings.synopsis: It was possible to enumerate configuration parameters of remote services.
findings.description: Nessus was able to obtain, via the SMB protocol, the launch parameters of each active service on the remote host (executable path, logon type, etc.).
findings.solution: Ensure that each service is configured properly.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB Last Logged On User Disclosure
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to identify the last logged on user on the remote host.
findings.description:
By connecting to the remote host with the supplied credentials, Nessus was able to identify the username associated with the last successful logon.

Microsoft documentation notes that interactive console logons change the DefaultUserName registry entry to be the last logged-on user.

findings.name: Windows Speculative Execution Configuration Check
findings.synopsis: The remote host has not properly mitigated a series of speculative execution vulnerabilities.
findings.description:
The remote host has not properly mitigated a series of known speculative execution vulnerabilities. It, therefore, may be affected by :
  - Branch Target Injection (BTI) (CVE-2017-5715)
  - Bounds Check Bypass (BCB) (CVE-2017-5753)
  - Rogue Data Cache Load (RDCL) (CVE-2017-5754)
  - Rogue System Register Read (RSRE) (CVE-2018-3640)
  - Speculative Store Bypass (SSB) (CVE-2018-3639)
  - L1 Terminal Fault (L1TF) (CVE-2018-3615, CVE-2018-3620, CVE-2018-3646)
  - Microarchitectural Data Sampling Uncacheable Memory (MDSUM) (CVE-2019-11091)
  - Microarchitectural Store Buffer Data Sampling (MSBDS) (CVE-2018-12126)
  - Microarchitectural Load Port Data Sampling (MLPDS) (CVE-2018-12127)
  - Microarchitectural Fill Buffer Data Sampling (MFBDS) (CVE-2018-12130)
  - TSX Asynchronous Abort (TAA) (CVE-2019-11135)

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB Service Enumeration
findings.synopsis: It is possible to enumerate remote services.
findings.description:
This plugin implements the SvcOpenSCManager() and SvcEnumServices() calls to obtain, using the SMB protocol, the list of active and inactive services of the remote host.

An attacker may use this feature to gain better knowledge of the remote host.
findings.solution: To prevent the listing of the services from being obtained, you should either have tight login restrictions, so that only trusted users can access your host, and/or you should filter incoming traffic to this port.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB Share Hosting Office Files
findings.synopsis: The remote share contains Office-related files.
findings.description: This plugin connects to the remotely accessible SMB shares and attempts to find office related files (such as .doc, .ppt, .xls, .pdf etc).
findings.solution: Make sure that the files containing confidential information have proper access controls set on them.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB Shares Access
findings.synopsis: It is possible to access a network share.
findings.description:
The remote has one or more Windows shares that can be accessed through the network with the given credentials.

Depending on the share rights, it may allow an attacker to read / write confidential data.
findings.solution: To restrict access under Windows, open Explorer, do a right click on each share, go to the 'sharing' tab, and click on 'permissions'.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB Shares Enumeration
findings.synopsis: It is possible to enumerate remote network shares.
findings.description: By connecting to the remote host, Nessus was able to enumerate the network share names.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows 'Administrators' Group User List
findings.synopsis: There is at least one user in the 'Administrators' group.
findings.description: Using the supplied credentials, it is possible to extract the member list of the 'Administrators' group. Members of this group have complete access to the remote system.
findings.solution: Verify that each member of the group should have this type of access.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB : Obtains the Password Policy
findings.synopsis: It is possible to retrieve the remote host's password policy using the supplied credentials.
findings.description: Using the supplied credentials it was possible to extract the password policy for the remote Windows host. The password policy must conform to the Informational System Policy.

findings.name: Windows Printer Driver Enumeration
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to enumerate one or more of the printer drivers on the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to enumerate one or more of the printer drivers on the remote host via WMI.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB Registry : Winlogon Cached Password Weakness
findings.synopsis: User credentials are stored in memory.
findings.description:
The registry key 'HKLM\Software\Microsoft\WindowsNT\CurrentVersion\ Winlogon\CachedLogonsCount' is not 0. Using a value greater than 0 for the CachedLogonsCount key indicates that the remote Windows host locally caches the passwords of the users when they login, in order to continue to allow the users to login in the case of the failure of the primary domain controller (PDC).

Cached logon credentials could be accessed by an attacker and subjected  to brute force attacks.
findings.solution: Consult Microsoft documentation and best practices.

findings.name: WinVerifyTrust Signature Validation CVE-2013-3900 Mitigation (EnableCertPaddingCheck)
findings.synopsis: The remote Windows host is potentially missing a mitigation for a remote code execution vulnerability.
findings.description:
The remote system may be in a vulnerable state to CVE-2013-3900 due to a missing or misconfigured registry keys:
    - HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Cryptography\Wintrust\Config\EnableCertPaddingCheck
    - HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Wow6432Node\Microsoft\Cryptography\Wintrust\Config\EnableCertPaddingCheck     An unauthenticated, remote attacker could exploit this, by sending specially crafted requests, to execute arbitrary code on an affected host.
findings.solution:
Add and enable registry value EnableCertPaddingCheck:
  - HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Cryptography\Wintrust\Config\EnableCertPaddingCheck

Additionally, on 64 Bit OS systems, Add and enable registry value EnableCertPaddingCheck:

  - HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Wow6432Node\Microsoft\Cryptography\Wintrust\Config\EnableCertPaddingCheck

findings.name: Microsoft Security Rollup Enumeration
findings.synopsis: This plugin enumerates installed Microsoft security rollups.
findings.description: Nessus was able to enumerate the Microsoft security rollups installed on the remote Windows host.

findings.name: DISM Package List (Windows)
findings.synopsis: Use DISM to extract package info from the host.

findings.name: Microsoft .NET Security Rollup Enumeration
findings.synopsis: This plugin enumerates installed Microsoft .NET security rollups.
findings.description: Nessus was able to enumerate the Microsoft .NET security rollups installed on the remote Windows host.

findings.name: Microsoft System Center Configuration Manager Client Installed

findings.description: The Microsoft System Center Configuration Manager client, a management system client, is installed on the remote Windows host.

findings.name: KB4017094: Security Update for the libjpeg Information Disclosure Vulnerability for Microsoft Silverlight 5 (April 2017)
findings.synopsis: A web application framework running on the remote host is affected by an information disclosure vulnerability.
findings.description: The version of Silverlight 5 installed on the remote Windows host is missing security update KB4017094. It is, therefore, affected by an information disclosure vulnerability in the open-source libjpeg image processing library due to improper handling of objects in memory. An unauthenticated, remote attacker can exploit this to disclose sensitive information that can be utilized to bypass ASLR security protections.

findings.name: KB4023307: Security Update for the Windows Uniscribe Remote Code Execution Vulnerability for Microsoft Silverlight 5 (June 2017)
findings.synopsis: A web application framework running on the remote host is affected by multiple remote code execution vulnerabilities.
findings.description:
The version of Silverlight 5 installed on the remote Windows host is missing security update KB4023307. It is, therefore, affected by multiple vulnerabilities :

  - A remote code execution vulnerability exists in     Windows Uniscribe software due to improper handling of     objects in memory. An unauthenticated, remote attacker     can exploit this, by convincing a user to visit a     specially crafted website or to open a specially crafted     document file, to execute arbitrary code in the context     of the current user. (CVE-2017-0283)

  - A remote code execution vulnerability exists in the     Windows font library due to improper handling of     embedded fonts. An unauthenticated, remote attacker can     exploit this, by convincing a user to visit a specially     crafted website or open a specially crafted Microsoft     document, to execute arbitrary code in the context of     the current user. (CVE-2017-8527)

findings.name: Microsoft Silverlight Unsupported Version Detection (Windows)
findings.synopsis: The remote host has an unsupported version of Microsoft Silverlight.
findings.description:
The installation of Microsoft Silverlight on the Windows host is no longer supported.

Lack of support implies that no new security patches for the product will be released by the vendor. As a result, it is likely to contain security vulnerabilities.

findings.name: Microsoft Silverlight Detection
findings.synopsis: The remote host has Microsoft Silverlight installed.
findings.description:
A version of Microsoft's Silverlight is installed on this host.

Microsoft Silverlight is a web application framework that provides functionalities similar to those in Adobe Flash, integrating multimedia, graphics, animations and interactivity into a single runtime environment.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows 'CWDIllegalInDllSearch' Registry Setting
findings.synopsis: CWDIllegalInDllSearch Settings: Improper settings could allow code execution attacks.
findings.description:
Windows Hosts can be hardened against DLL hijacking attacks by  setting the The 'CWDIllegalInDllSearch' registry entry in to  one of the following settings:

  - 0xFFFFFFFF (Removes the current working directory     from the default DLL search order)

  - 1 (Blocks a DLL Load from the current working     directory if the current working directory is set     to a WebDAV folder)

  - 2 (Blocks a DLL Load from the current working     directory if the current working directory is set     to a remote folder)

findings.name: Windows DNS Server Enumeration
findings.synopsis: Nessus enumerated the DNS servers being used by the remote Windows host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to enumerate the DNS servers configured on the remote Windows host by looking in the registry.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Mounted Devices
findings.synopsis: It is possible to get a list of mounted devices that may have been connected to the remote system in the past.
findings.description: By connecting to the remote host with the supplied credentials, this plugin enumerates mounted devices that have been connected to the remote host in the past.
findings.solution: Make sure that the mounted drives agree with your organization's acceptable use and security policies.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Portable Devices
findings.synopsis: It is possible to get a list of portable devices that may have been connected to the remote system in the past.
findings.description: By connecting to the remote host with the supplied credentials, this plugin enumerates portable devices that have been connected to the remote host in the past.
findings.solution: Make sure that use of the portable devices agrees with your organization's acceptable use and security policies.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows USB Device Usage Report
findings.synopsis: It was possible to get a list of USB devices that may have been connected to the remote system in the past.
findings.description: Using the supplied credentials, this plugin enumerates USB devices that have been connected to the remote Windows host in the past.
findings.solution: Make sure that the use of USB drives is in accordance with your organization's security policy.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Installed Software Enumeration (credentialed check)
findings.synopsis: It is possible to enumerate installed software.
findings.description:
This plugin lists software potentially installed on the remote host by crawling the registry entries in :

  HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall   HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Updates

Note that these entries do not necessarily mean the applications are actually installed on the remote host - they may have been left behind by uninstallers, or the associated files may have been manually removed.
findings.solution: Remove any applications that are not compliant with your organization's acceptable use and security policies.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Startup Software Enumeration
findings.synopsis: It is possible to enumerate startup software.
findings.description:
This plugin lists software that is configured to run on system startup by crawling the registry entries in :

  - HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
    -     HKLM\SOFTWARE\Wow6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersi     on\Run
findings.solution: Review the list of applications and remove any that are not compliant with your organization's acceptable use and security policies.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Network Adapters
findings.synopsis: Identifies the network adapters installed on the remote host.
findings.description: Using the supplied credentials, this plugin enumerates and reports the installed network adapters on the remote Windows host.
findings.solution: Make sure that all of the installed network adapters agrees with your organization's acceptable use and security policies.

findings.name: SMB Use Host SID to Enumerate Local Users
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to enumerate local users.
findings.description: Using the host security identifier (SID), Nessus was able to enumerate local users on the remote Windows system.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB LsaQueryInformationPolicy Function SID Enumeration
findings.synopsis: It is possible to obtain the host SID for the remote host.
findings.description:
By emulating the call to LsaQueryInformationPolicy(), it was possible to obtain the host SID (Security Identifier).

The host SID can then be used to get the list of local users.
findings.solution:
You can prevent anonymous lookups of the host SID by setting the 'RestrictAnonymous' registry setting to an appropriate value.

Refer to the 'See also' section for guidance.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Installed Software Version Enumeration
findings.synopsis: Enumerates installed software versions.
findings.description:
This plugin enumerates the installed software version by interrogating information obtained from various registry entries and files on disk. This plugin provides a best guess at the software version and a confidence level for that version.

Note that the versions detected here do not necessarily indicate the actual installed version nor do they necessarily mean that the application is actually installed on the remote host. In some cases there may be artifacts left behind by uninstallers on the system.
findings.solution: Remove any applications that are not compliant with your organization's acceptable use and security policies.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Logged On Users
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to determine the logged on users from the registry
findings.description: Using the HKU registry, Nessus was able to enuemrate the SIDs of logged on users

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB : WSUS Client Configured
findings.synopsis: The remote Windows host is utilizing a WSUS server.
findings.description: The remote host is configured to utilize a Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) server.
findings.solution: Verify the remote host is configured to utilize the correct WSUS server.

findings.name: Server Message Block (SMB) Protocol Version 1 Enabled
findings.synopsis: The remote Windows host supports the SMBv1 protocol.
findings.description: The remote Windows host supports Server Message Block Protocol version 1 (SMBv1). Microsoft recommends that users discontinue the use of SMBv1 due to the lack of security features that were included in later SMB versions. Additionally, the Shadow Brokers group reportedly has an exploit that affects SMB; however, it is unknown if the exploit affects SMBv1 or another version. In response to this, US-CERT recommends that users disable SMBv1 per SMB best practices to mitigate these potential issues.
findings.solution: Disable SMBv1 according to the vendor instructions in Microsoft KB2696547. Additionally, block SMB directly by blocking TCP port 445 on all network boundary devices. For SMB over the NetBIOS API, block TCP ports 137 / 139 and UDP ports 137 / 138 on all network boundary devices.

findings.name: Windows Store Application Enumeration
findings.synopsis: It is possible to obtain the list of applications installed from the Windows Store.
findings.description: This plugin connects to the remote Windows host with the supplied credentials and uses WMI and Powershell to enumerate applications installed on the host from the Windows Store.

findings.name: SMB Signing not required
findings.synopsis: Signing is not required on the remote SMB server.
findings.description: Signing is not required on the remote SMB server. An unauthenticated, remote attacker can exploit this to conduct man-in-the-middle attacks against the SMB server.
findings.solution: Enforce message signing in the host's configuration. On Windows, this is found in the policy setting 'Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)'. On Samba, the setting is called 'server signing'. See the 'see also' links for further details.

findings.name: Windows Product Key Retrieval
findings.synopsis: This plugin retrieves the Windows Product key of the remote Windows host.
findings.description: Using the supplied credentials, Nessus was able to obtain the retrieve the Windows host's partial product key'.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows NTLMSSP Authentication Request Remote Network Name Disclosure
findings.synopsis: It is possible to obtain the network name of the remote host.
findings.description:
The remote host listens on tcp port 445 and replies to SMB requests.

By sending an NTLMSSP authentication request it is possible to obtain the name of the remote system and the name of its domain.

findings.name: Microsoft Internet Explorer Version Detection
findings.synopsis: Internet Explorer is installed on the remote host.
findings.description: The remote Windows host contains Internet Explorer, a web browser created by Microsoft.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB Registry : OS Version and Processor Architecture
findings.synopsis: It was possible to determine the processor architecture, build lab strings, and Windows OS version installed on the remote system.
findings.description: Nessus was able to determine the processor architecture, build lab strings, and the Windows OS version installed on the remote system by connecting to the remote registry with the supplied credentials.

findings.name: Windows Disabled Command Prompt Enumeration
findings.synopsis: This plugin determines if the DisableCMD policy is enabled or disabled on the remote host for each local user.
findings.description:
The remote host may employ the DisableCMD policy on a per user basis. Enumerated local  users may have the following registry key:
 'HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System\DisableCMD'

  - Unset or 0: The command prompt is enabled normally.
  - 1: The command promt is disabled.
  - 2: The command prompt is disabled however windows batch processing is allowed.

findings.name: SMB Use Domain SID to Enumerate Users
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to enumerate domain users.
findings.description: Using the domain security identifier (SID), Nessus was able to enumerate the domain users on the remote Windows system.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB LsaQueryInformationPolicy Function NULL Session Domain SID Enumeration
findings.synopsis: It was possible to obtain the domain SID.
findings.description:
By making or emulating a call to LsaQueryInformationPolicy(), it was possible to obtain the domain SID (Security Identifier).

The domain SID can then be used to get the list of users of the domain.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB Registry Remotely Accessible
findings.synopsis: Access the remote Windows Registry.
findings.description: It was possible to access the remote Windows Registry using the login / password combination used for the Windows local checks (SMB tests).

findings.name: WMI Available
findings.synopsis: WMI queries can be made against the remote host.
findings.description:
The supplied credentials can be used to make WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) requests against the remote host over DCOM. 

These requests can be used to gather information about the remote host, such as its current state, network interface configuration, etc.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB Log In Possible
findings.synopsis: It was possible to log into the remote host.
findings.description:
The remote host is running a Microsoft Windows operating system or Samba, a CIFS/SMB server for Unix. It was possible to log into it using one of the following accounts :

- Guest account
- Supplied credentials

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB NativeLanManager Remote System Information Disclosure
findings.synopsis: It was possible to obtain information about the remote operating system.
findings.description: Nessus was able to obtain the remote operating system name and version (Windows and/or Samba) by sending an authentication request to port 139 or 445. Note that this plugin requires SMB to be enabled on the host.

findings.name: Windows NetBIOS / SMB Remote Host Information Disclosure
findings.synopsis: It was possible to obtain the network name of the remote host.
findings.description:
The remote host is listening on UDP port 137 or TCP port 445, and replies to NetBIOS nbtscan or SMB requests.

Note that this plugin gathers information to be used in other plugins, but does not itself generate a report.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB Service Detection
findings.synopsis: A file / print sharing service is listening on the remote host.
findings.description: The remote service understands the CIFS (Common Internet File System) or Server Message Block (SMB) protocol, used to provide shared access to files, printers, etc between nodes on a network.

findings.name: Intel CPUID detection
findings.synopsis: The processor CPUID was detected on the remote host.
findings.description: The CPUID of the Intel processor was detected on the remote host.

findings.name: Traceroute Information
findings.synopsis: It was possible to obtain traceroute information.
findings.description: Makes a traceroute to the remote host.

findings.name: Open Port Re-check
findings.synopsis: Previously open ports are now closed.
findings.description:
One of several ports that were previously open are now closed or unresponsive.

There are several possible reasons for this :

  - The scan may have caused a service to freeze or stop     running.

  - An administrator may have stopped a particular service     during the scanning process.

This might be an availability problem related to the following :

  - A network outage has been experienced during the scan,     and the remote network cannot be reached anymore by the     scanner.

  - This scanner may has been blacklisted by the system     administrator or by an automatic intrusion detection /     prevention system that detected the scan.

  - The remote host is now down, either because a user     turned it off during the scan or because a select denial     of service was effective.

In any case, the audit of the remote host might be incomplete and may need to be done again.
findings.solution:
Steps to resolve this issue include :

- Increase checks_read_timeout and/or reduce max_checks.

- Disable any IPS during the Nessus scan

findings.name: SMB Registry : Stop the Registry Service after the scan (WMI)
findings.synopsis: The registry service was stopped after the scan.
findings.description: To perform a full credentialed scan, Nessus needs the ability to connect to the remote registry service (RemoteRegistry). If the service is down and if Nessus automatically enabled the registry for the duration of the scan, this plugins will stop it afterwards.

findings.name: Nessus Scan Information
findings.synopsis: This plugin displays information about the Nessus scan.
findings.description:
This plugin displays, for each tested host, information about the scan itself :

  - The version of the plugin set.
  - The type of scanner (Nessus or Nessus Home).
  - The version of the Nessus Engine.
  - The port scanner(s) used.
  - The port range scanned.
  - The ping round trip time 
  - Whether credentialed or third-party patch management     checks are possible.
  - Whether the display of superseded patches is enabled
  - The date of the scan.
  - The duration of the scan.
  - The number of hosts scanned in parallel.
  - The number of checks done in parallel.

findings.name: Common Platform Enumeration (CPE)
findings.synopsis: It was possible to enumerate CPE names that matched on the remote system.
findings.description:
By using information obtained from a Nessus scan, this plugin reports CPE (Common Platform Enumeration) matches for various hardware and software products found on a host. 

Note that if an official CPE is not available for the product, this plugin computes the best possible CPE based on the information available from the scan.

findings.name: Patch Report
findings.synopsis: The remote host is missing several patches.
findings.description:
The remote host is missing one or more security patches. This plugin lists the newest version of each patch to install to make sure the remote host is up-to-date.

Note: Because the 'Show missing patches that have been superseded' setting in your scan policy depends on this plugin, it will always run and cannot be disabled.

findings.name: Microsoft Internet Explorer Installed
findings.synopsis: A web browser is installed on the remote Windows host.
findings.description: Microsoft Internet Explorer, a web browser bundled with Microsoft Windows, is installed on the remote Windows host.

findings.name: Windows Language Settings Detection
findings.synopsis: This plugin enumerates language files on a windows host.
findings.description: By connecting to the remote host with the supplied credentials, this plugin enumerates language IDs listed on the host.

findings.name: Device Type
findings.synopsis: It is possible to guess the remote device type.
findings.description: Based on the remote operating system, it is possible to determine what the remote system type is (eg: a printer, router, general-purpose computer, etc).

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Last Boot Time
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to collect the remote host's last boot time in a human readable format.
findings.description: Nessus was able to collect and report the remote host's last boot time as an ISO 8601 timestamp.

findings.name: OS Identification
findings.synopsis: It is possible to guess the remote operating system.
findings.description: Using a combination of remote probes (e.g., TCP/IP, SMB, HTTP, NTP, SNMP, etc.), it is possible to guess the name of the remote operating system in use. It is also possible sometimes to guess the version of the operating system.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Installed
findings.synopsis: The remote host is running Microsoft Windows.
findings.description: The remote host is running Microsoft Windows.

findings.name: Windows Defender Installed
findings.synopsis: Windows Defender is installed on the remote Windows host.
findings.description: Windows Defender, an antivirus component of Microsoft Windows is installed  on the remote Windows host.

findings.name: Trend Micro Deep Security Agent Installed (Windows)
findings.synopsis: Trend Micro Deep Security Agent is installed on the remote Windows host.
findings.description: Trend Micro Deep Security Agent which provides application control, anti-malware, web reputation service, firewall, intrusion prevention, integrity monitoring, and log inspection protection is installed on the remote Windows host.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows - Users Information : Never Changed Password
findings.synopsis: At least one user has never changed his or her password.
findings.description: Using the supplied credentials, Nessus was able to list users who have never changed their passwords.
findings.solution: Allow or require users to change their passwords regularly.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows - Users Information : User Has Never Logged In
findings.synopsis: At least one user has never logged into his or her account.
findings.description: Using the supplied credentials, Nessus was able to list users who have never logged into their accounts.
findings.solution: Delete accounts that are not needed.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows - Users Information : Disabled Accounts
findings.synopsis: At least one user account has been disabled.
findings.description: Using the supplied credentials, Nessus was able to list user accounts that have been disabled.
findings.solution: Delete accounts that are no longer needed.

findings.name: Host Active Directory Configuration (Windows)
findings.synopsis: The Windows host is joined to an Active Directory domain.
findings.description:
The Windows host is joined to an Active Directory domain and it was possible to retrieve certain Active Directory configuration attributes, including:

Computer information in AD:
  - Common Name
  - DNS Name
  - Distinguished Name
  - Domain Role
  - Object SID
  - SamAccountName

AD domain and forest information:
  - Domain FQDN
  - Domain GUID
  - Domain NetBIOS Name
  - Domain SID
  - Forest FQDN

findings.name: Local Administrator Password Solution Installed
findings.synopsis: A password management utility is installed on the remote Windows host.
findings.description: Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS), a password management utility, is installed on the remote Windows host.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows ARP Table
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to collect and report ARP table information from the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to collect ARP table information from the remote Windows host and generate a report as a CSV attachment.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Environment Variables
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to collect and report environment variables from the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to collect system and active account environment variables on the remote Windows host and generate a report as a CSV attachment.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Hosts File
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to collect the hosts file from the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to collect the hosts file from the remote Windows host and report it as attachment.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows DNS Cache
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to collect and report DNS cache information from the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to collect details of the DNS cache from the remote Windows host and generate a report as a CSV attachment.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows PowerShell Execution Policy
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to collect and report the PowerShell execution policy for the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to collect and report the PowerShell execution policy for the remote Windows host.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows SMB Sessions
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to collect and report SMB session information from the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to collect details of SMB sessions from the remote Windows host and generate a report as a CSV attachment.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Scripting Host Settings
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to collect and report the Windows scripting host settings from the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to collect system and user level Windows scripting host settings from the remote Windows host and generate a report as a CSV attachment.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows NetBIOS over TCP/IP Info
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to collect and report NBT information from the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to collect details for NetBIOS over TCP/IP from the remote Windows host and generate a report as a CSV attachment.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Time Zone Information
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to collect and report time zone information from the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to collect time zone information from the remote Windows host and generate a report as a CSV attachment.

findings.name: Microsoft Remote Desktop Connection Installed
findings.synopsis: A graphical interface connection utility is installed on the remote Windows host
findings.description: Microsoft Remote Desktop Connection (also known as Remote Desktop Protocol or Terminal Services Client) is installed on the remote Windows host.

findings.name: SMB QuickFixEngineering (QFE) Enumeration
findings.synopsis: The remote host has quick-fix engineering updates installed.
findings.description: By connecting to the host with the supplied credentials, this plugin enumerates quick-fix engineering updates installed on the remote host via the registry.

findings.name: Windows Enumerate Accounts
findings.synopsis: Enumerate Windows accounts.
findings.description: Enumerate Windows accounts.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows - Local Users Information : Never Changed Passwords
findings.synopsis: At least one local user has never changed his or her password.

findings.name: Enumerate the PATH Variables
findings.synopsis: Enumerates the PATH variable of the current scan user.
findings.description: Enumerates the PATH variables of the current scan user.
findings.solution: Ensure that directories listed here are in line with corporate policy.

findings.synopsis: The manufacturer can be identified from the Ethernet OUI.
findings.description: Each ethernet MAC address starts with a 24-bit Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI). These OUIs are registered by IEEE.

findings.name: Ethernet MAC Addresses
findings.synopsis: This plugin gathers MAC addresses from various sources and consolidates them into a list.
findings.description: This plugin gathers MAC addresses discovered from both remote probing of the host (e.g. SNMP and Netbios) and from running local checks (e.g. ifconfig). It then consolidates the MAC addresses into a single, unique, and uniform list.

findings.name: Device Hostname
findings.synopsis: It was possible to determine the remote system hostname.
findings.description: This plugin reports a device's hostname collected via SSH or WMI.

findings.name: Additional DNS Hostnames
findings.synopsis: Nessus has detected potential virtual hosts.
findings.description:
Hostnames different from the current hostname have been collected by miscellaneous plugins. Nessus has generated a list of hostnames that point to the remote host. Note that these are only the alternate hostnames for vhosts discovered on a web server.

Different web servers may be hosted on name-based virtual hosts.
findings.solution:
If you want to test them, re-scan using the special vhost syntax, such as :

www.example.com[192.0.32.10]

findings.name: Application Compatibility Cache
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to gather application compatibility settings on the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to generate a report on the application compatibility cache on the remote Windows host.

findings.name: Internet Explorer Typed URLs
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to enumerate URLs that were manually typed into the Internet Explorer address bar.
findings.description: Nessus was able to generate a list URLs that were manually typed into the Internet Explorer address bar.

findings.name: Windows Explorer Recently Executed Programs
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to enumerate recently executed programs on the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to find evidence of program execution using Windows Explorer registry logs and settings.

findings.name: MUICache Program Execution History
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to enumerate recently executed programs on the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to query the MUIcache registry key to find evidence of program execution.

findings.name: OpenSaveMRU History
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to enumerate opened and saved files on the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to generate a report on files that were opened using the shell dialog box or saved using the shell dialog box. This is the box that appears when you attempt to save a document or open a document in Windows Explorer.

findings.name: Recent File History
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to enumerate recently opened files on the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to gather evidence of files opened by file type from the remote host.

findings.name: Recycle Bin Files
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to enumerate files in the recycle bin on the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to generate a list of all files found in $Recycle.Bin subdirectories.

findings.name: User Shell Folders Settings
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to find the folder paths for user folders on the remote host.
findings.description:
Nessus was able to gather a list of settings from the target system that store common user folder locations. A few of the more common locations are listed below :

  - Administrative Tools
  - AppData
  - Cache
  - CD Burning
  - Cookies
  - Desktop

  - Fonts
  - History
  - Local AppData
  - My Music
  - My Pictures
  - My Video
  - NetHood
  - Personal
  - PrintHood
  - Programs
  - Recent
  - SendTo
  - Start Menu
  - Startup
  - Templates

findings.name: User Download Folder Files
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to enumerate downloaded files on the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to generate a report of all files listed in the default user download folder.

findings.name: UserAssist Execution History
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to enumerate program execution history on the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to gather evidence from the UserAssist registry key that has a list of programs that have been executed.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Process Module Information
findings.synopsis: Use WMI to obtain running process module information.
findings.description:
Report details on the running processes modules on the machine.

This plugin is informative only and could be used for forensic investigation, malware detection, and to that confirm your system processes conform to your system policies.

findings.name: Microsoft Windows Process Information
findings.synopsis: Use WMI to obtain running process information.
findings.description:
Report details on the running processes on the machine.

This plugin is informative only and could be used for forensic investigation, malware detection, and to confirm that your system processes conform to your system policies.

findings.name: BIOS Info (WMI)
findings.synopsis: The BIOS info could be read.
findings.description: It is possible to get information about the BIOS via the host's WMI interface.

findings.name: Host Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) Resolution
findings.synopsis: It was possible to resolve the name of the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to resolve the fully qualified domain name (FQDN) of the remote host.

findings.name: Computer Manufacturer Information (WMI)
findings.synopsis: It is possible to obtain the name of the remote computer manufacturer.
findings.description: By making certain WMI queries, it is possible to obtain the model of the remote computer as well as the name of its manufacturer and its serial number.

findings.name: Windows ComputerSystemProduct Enumeration (WMI)
findings.synopsis: It is possible to obtain product information from the remote host using WMI.
findings.description: By querying the WMI class 'Win32_ComputerSystemProduct', it is possible to extract product information about the computer system such as UUID, IdentifyingNumber, vendor, etc.

findings.name: Windows Display Driver Enumeration
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to enumerate one or more of the display drivers on the remote host.
findings.description: Nessus was able to enumerate one or more of the display drivers on the remote host via WMI.

findings.name: WMI QuickFixEngineering (QFE) Enumeration
findings.synopsis: The remote Windows host has quick-fix engineering updates installed.
findings.description: By connecting to the remote host with the supplied credentials, this plugin enumerates quick-fix engineering updates installed on the remote host via WMI.

findings.name: Enumerate Local Group Memberships
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to connect to a host via SMB to retrieve a list of local Groups and their Members.
findings.description: Nessus was able to connect to a host via SMB to retrieve a list of local Groups and their Members.

findings.name: Logical Drive Insecure Filesystem Enumeration (WMI)
findings.synopsis: The remote host is using an insecure filesystem.
findings.description: By making certain WMI queries, it is possible to extract the list of logical drives of the remote host that do not use NTFS.
findings.solution: Migrate any reported filesystems to NTFS.

findings.name: USB Drives Enumeration (WMI)
findings.synopsis: It is possible to obtain the list of USB drives on the remote host.
findings.description: By connecting to the remote host with the supplied credentials, it is possible to extract the list of USB drives of the remote host and the drive name attached to each.
findings.solution: Make sure that use of external USB drives matches your organization's security policy.

findings.name: WMI Windows Feature Enumeration
findings.synopsis: It is possible to enumerate Windows features using WMI.
findings.description:
Nessus was able to enumerate the server features of the remote host by querying the 'Win32_ServerFeature' class of the '\Root\cimv2' WMI namespace for Windows Server versions or the 'Win32_OptionalFeature' class of the '\Root\cimv2' WMI namespace for Windows Desktop versions.

Note that Features can only be enumerated for Windows 7 and later for desktop versions.

findings.name: Netstat Connection Information
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to parse the results of the 'netstat' command on the remote host.
findings.description:
The remote host has listening ports or established connections that Nessus was able to extract from the results of the 'netstat' command.

Note: The output for this plugin can be very long, and is not shown by default. To display it, enable verbose reporting in scan settings.

findings.name: Enumerate Users via WMI
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to connect to a host via SMB to retrieve a list of users using WMI.
findings.description: Nessus was able to connect to a host via SMB to retrieve a list of users using WMI.  Only identities that the authenticated SMB user has permissions to view will be retrieved by this plugin.

findings.name: Network Interfaces Enumeration (WMI)
findings.synopsis: Nessus was able to obtain the list of network interfaces on the remote host.
findings.description:
Nessus was able, via WMI queries, to extract a list of network interfaces on the remote host and the IP addresses attached to them.
Note that this plugin only enumerates IPv6 addresses for systems running Windows Vista or later.

findings.name: SMB Registry : Start the Registry Service during the scan (WMI)
findings.synopsis: The registry service was enabled for the duration of the scan.
findings.description:
To perform a full credentialed scan, Nessus needs the ability to connect to the remote registry service (RemoteRegistry). If the service is down, this plugin will attempt to start for the duration of the scan.

For this plugin to work, you need to select the option 'Start the Remote Registry service during the scan' on the credentials page when you add your Windows credentials.

findings.name: ICMP Timestamp Request Remote Date Disclosure
findings.synopsis: It is possible to determine the exact time set on the remote host.
findings.description:
The remote host answers to an ICMP timestamp request.  This allows an attacker to know the date that is set on the targeted machine, which may assist an unauthenticated, remote attacker in defeating time-based authentication protocols.

Timestamps returned from machines running Windows Vista / 7 / 2008 / 2008 R2 are deliberately incorrect, but usually within 1000 seconds of the actual system time.
findings.solution: Filter out the ICMP timestamp requests (13), and the outgoing ICMP timestamp replies (14).
